claims.text: The initial nanoparticles contain five or more metals in near-equal atomic ratios and are single-phase disordered solid solutions.
The balance between configurational entropy and kinetic barriers to atomic diffusion governs structural and chemical stability in initially single-phase HEA nanoparticles.
High configurational entropy reduces the thermodynamic driving force for precipitation or phase separation.
Low atomic diffusion kinetically restrains precipitate formation.
The thermodynamic driving force for clustering and phase separation increases with temperature because atomic mobility is enhanced.
If entropy-induced stabilization does not dominate, local ordering or phase separation occurs.
Atomic-size mismatches and bonding differences influence local ordering and clustering.
At moderate temperatures, mixing entropy stabilizes the disordered solid solution and impedes diffusion-mediated clustering.
At higher temperatures, enhanced atomic mobility can overcome kinetic barriers and permit ordering or phase separation when the enthalpic driving force is sufficiently high.
Diffusion activation energy is affected by atomic mismatch and interaction strengths.
Minimal differences in atomic sizes and bonding energies maximize high-entropy stabilization.
Nanoparticles with minimal atomic-size and bonding-energy differences will retain a disordered single-phase structure with only limited local ordering across 473–1923 K.
Comparable nanoparticles with more pronounced enthalpic differences will develop detectable segregation or local ordering near 1923 K.
The initial room-temperature baseline is a chemically homogeneous, single-phase nanoparticle state verified by diffraction and microscopy.
The prediction is limited to inert or controlled atmospheres with minimal oxidation, contamination, external reactions, and non-equilibrium cooling effects.
The temperature at which clustering begins depends on atomic-size mismatches and local bonding differences.
Strain or stress under catalytic operating conditions may alter the balance between stabilization and clustering.
A controlled heating cycle from 473 K to 1923 K under inert atmosphere, monitored by XRD, TEM, and DSC, can test for phase segregation, ordering, clustering, and phase-transition events.
Observation of separation, clustering, or ordering in both comparison sets anywhere within 473–1923 K would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.

contradictions.description: The two sets are described as having identical overall compositions, but the second set is also said to receive an off-stoichiometric elemental addition, which necessarily changes its composition.
The boundary says temperature is the only modulated variable, whereas the proposed comparison also changes composition and atomic mismatch.

The hypothesis treats enhanced mobility as increasing the thermodynamic driving force for separation, while the mechanism more appropriately treats mobility as overcoming a kinetic barrier in the presence of a separate enthalpic driving force.

The hypothesis already permits phase separation when kinetic or entropy stabilization is insufficient, so observing separation in both sets does not by itself falsify the claim that entropy and diffusion barriers govern stability.
